questions.question: In ZrNbTaW refractory high-entropy alloys processed by powder metallurgy, does extending milling time beyond 50 hours further increase hardness, or does the onset of excessive oxide/carbide contamination cause property degradation?
questions.rationale: The study shows hardness increases up to 50 hours but notes contamination risks; determining the upper limit of effective milling prevents process failure.
questions.decision_use: To define the maximum viable milling duration for industrial scaling of this alloy system.
answer_requirements: Measure hardness and phase composition of samples milled for >50 hours (e.g., 75h) and compare to 50h baseline.
Quantify oxide/carbide fraction using XRD and EDS.
evidence_spans: The RHEA produced by mechanical alloying of powders for a period of 50 h presented the highest hardness of 675.7 ± 9.8 HV0.2 among all alloys
increased milling times of the powders lead to the formation of a higher fraction of ZrC after sintering

questions.question: For ZrNbTaW RHEAs, does the hardness gain from Hall-Petch strengthening at intermediate milling times outweigh the embrittlement risk from carbide formation observed after 3 hours?
questions.rationale: The study links hardness to grain refinement and carbide formation but does not explicitly weigh the trade-off between strength gain and ductility loss at early milling stages.
questions.decision_use: To decide if early-stage milling (3-10h) is viable for applications requiring toughness, or if longer milling is strictly necessary.
answer_requirements: Measure fracture toughness and tensile ductility of 3h, 10h, and 50h milled samples.
Correlate ZrC volume fraction with impact energy.
evidence_spans: carbide formation was detected in the sintered bulks as early as after 3 h of powder milling
due to the possible Hall–Petch strengthening effect
